articles.title: Military widows' future stuck in partisan brawl over veteran benefits
articles.summary: The fight has little to do with grieving spouses, but they're caught in the middle of a bigger battle over how veterans should get compensated for their serv...
articles.body:
A House brawl over veteran benefits could ruin the last, best chance for military widows to fix a decades-old law that penalizes them for falling in love again.

The fight has little to do with grieving spouses, who want to overturn a 70-year-old rule that strips away support benefits when they remarry. But they're caught in the middle of a much bigger battle over how veterans should get compensated for their service.

Republicans have proposed funding this and other benefits by pulling money from future disability payments for veterans with sleep apnea and hearing issues. Democrats argue that sets a dangerous precedent and betrays promises to take care of wounded troops.

The standoff comes as U.S. troop casualties in the Iran war mount and Republicans wrestle with the Trump administration's plans for a record-breaking defense budget — none of which is slated for a military widows fix. And with lawmakers unable to resolve their fight over paying for new veterans' benefits, it's increasingly likely Congress will once again fail to fix the problem.

"It's really difficult that this country makes widows have to calculate financial consequences before they're allowed to love somebody again," said Kaanan Mackey-Fugler, whose first husband, Iowa National Guard Staff Sgt. Matthew Mackey, died in a 2010 accident just weeks after returning from an active-duty deployment to Iraq.

The mother of five didn't plan to remarry. But seven years later, she fell in love and decided she needed to move on with her life. It cost her tens of thousands of dollars.

"It has gotten to the point where my new husband and I have had conversations about whether to get divorced, just to get those benefits back," she said.

When a servicemember dies, their spouse receives monthly payments from the military and Department of Veterans Affairs, totaling around $1,700. But when Congress originally approved the program in the 1950s, lawmakers included a provision that the government would discontinue checks if that spouse gets remarried before 55.

Advocates note that many states had rules at the time about women opening their own bank accounts and holding credit cards. Today, nearly half of military families are dual income households.

Congress "has an opportunity to end the unfair penalties placed on surviving families," said Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kansas), sponsor of two bills that would fix the remarriage issue. "Military service is a family service."

A group of 179 House lawmakers and 60 senators — including 41 chamber Democrats — have signed onto Moran's stand-alone legislation dubbed the Love Lives On Act to address the remarriage problem. But similar efforts over the last decade have faced the same congressional obstacle: cost.

VA estimates have put the expense of addressing the issue at up to $4 billion over the next decade. And appropriators have jousted over whether VA or Defense Department funds should cover the bill.

Moran, the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee chair, and House Veterans' Affairs Chair Mike Bost (R-Ill.) proposed a solution this year in the Take Care of America's Veterans Act . It uses $57 billion in projected savings to erase the remarriage penalty and pay for a host of other new veterans payouts.

But the source of those savings is a years-old proposal to limit money awarded for new veterans' disability claims related to tinnitus and sleep apnea. Groups like the Veterans of Foreign Wars and Disabled American Veterans have decried that move as stealing from one group of military beneficiaries to boost others' wallets.

Other groups — like the Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors — note that Veterans Affairs is set to make the disability changes regardless of the fate of the sweeping veterans benefits bill.

"Every Congress we get very close on this," said Ashlynne Haycock-Lohmann, director of government and legislative affairs for the nonprofit. "This is the closest and best chance we've ever had to really get this done. And it's definitely our only chance in this Congress."

Democratic leaders have strongly supported passing the Love Lives On Act on its own, but not as part of the Take Care of America's Veterans Act. They have also questioned whether the VA disability changes should or will go through.

Critics of the bigger bill say it is misguided, preferring to keep trying to pass the benefits expansions as individual bills.

Republicans appeared poised to pass the measure until July , when a handful of GOP House members raised concerns highlighted by the critics. Speaker Mike Johnson blamed "misinformation" on the defections and said leaders would work with bill sponsors to win over the needed votes this fall.

House lawmakers are eyeing mid-September for another vote, one they hope will have enough GOP backing to advance the issue.

Bost called it "the No. 1 priority" for his committee and most veterans advocates. He also said the measure will "do good for every corner of the veteran community by addressing the issues we have been working on for years," like the remarriage penalty.

If the House can pass the measure in the next few weeks, Senate Republican leaders have promised to fast-track the legislation in an effort to send it to the president's desk by the end of the year. If House lawmakers can't, the measure will likely be shelved until the next Congress.

Spouses like Loretta Booker are hoping for a positive outcome. She lost her husband, Petty Officer 1st Class Corwyn A. Booker Jr., to a sudden illness in 2019. She never thought she would remarry, but she became engaged in January.

Now she's trying to figure out how long she can wait to get married. If she holds out five more years, she'll turn 55 and avoid the financial penalties. But her son will also be 18 by then, and her new husband won't have the same opportunity to adopt him.

"I'm not getting a replacement husband," she said. "I will always be my late husband's widow. But I also know he would want me to move on, … and you shouldn't have to choose between moving on and financial security."

It’s been 30 years since Raising Cane’s first opened in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Since then, the company has brought its chicken fingers and Cane’s Sauce to more than 950 locations in 44 states, the District of Columbia, and Guam.

An exact opening date hasn’t been set for the Wharf location, but Raising Cane’s has confirmed when others will open their doors in September:

A handful of other future locations are listed as opening soon on the Raising Cane’s website, but no scheduled date has been released yet:

Local reports show a location is also in the works in Springfield, Oregon. A representative previously confirmed to Nexstar’s KRON that the company hopes to open new locations in Rohnert Park and Napa , both north of San Francisco, next year.

Officials in Colonie , New York, and West Manchester Township , Pennsylvania, have also given Raising Cane’s approval to build new locations in their towns. It’s unclear when these restaurants could open.

articles.title: We can create the recycling system Americans deserve
articles.summary: Congress has a rare, bipartisan opportunity to modernize America’s recycling system.
articles.body:
Every day, millions of people across the country rinse a bottle, break down a box or drop a plastic tub in their recycling bin, hoping that it will end up in the right place. The reality is often the opposite.

A recent op-ed in The Hill got the diagnosis right. America’s recycling system is outdated. But the prescription is wrong. We agree on the problem. We don’t agree on the solution.

Today, nearly 10,000 different recycling systems operate across the U.S. states, counties and cities across the country each have their own definitions of what belongs in the recycling bin and how packaging should be labeled. A container accepted for recycling in one city may not be accepted just a few towns over, while a recycling claim printed on one package may not qualify under another state’s rules.

This patchwork of regulations does more than just confuse consumers and stifle recycling rates. It also creates real costs for businesses trying to invest in better packaging and technology. As a result, this fragmented landscape makes long-term investment in new recycling technology and recycled content harder to achieve.

Congress has a rare, bipartisan opportunity to modernize America’s recycling system. The Recycled Materials Attribution Act and the PACK Act are currently under consideration by the House Energy and Commerce Committee. Together, these bills would resolve both of these issues with national standards for recyclable and recycled content claims and ensure consumer transparency through independent, third-party certification. This distinction matters. It ensures a recyclable label would mean the same thing, whether a product is purchased in Florida or Oregon.

The legislation also extends to newer, complementary technologies, known as advanced recycling. These technologies can process materials that traditional recycling cannot, like multilayer wrappers and plastic tubs used to keep food and household products safe. Advanced recycling does not replace traditional recycling — it extends what the current system can recover.

A recent report by the Progressive Policy Institute found that emerging recycling technologies, paired with traditional mechanical recycling, could more than double U.S. plastic recycling rates and save states and local municipalities hundreds of millions of dollars per year. These common-sense, practical solutions are the first step toward removing the barriers that have held back innovation at scale in recycling, allowing companies to recover more materials for reuse and keep them out of landfills.

Another crucial part of this legislation would require the Federal Trade Commission to update its Green Guides, which have not kept pace with the packaging and labeling innovations already in the marketplace. Modernizing that guidance would give companies one clear playbook to design and market products, instead of 50 different sets of rules.

The stakes also extend beyond any single recycling bin. Recycling supports 650,000 American jobs and generates $37.8 billion in wages annually. Every improvement made to our country’s recycling system plays a role in the economy. A confused consumer and lack of modernized technology leave that value on the table.

Through the Recycling Leadership Council , a coalition of businesses and stakeholders working across the value chain, we are already collaborating with partners to reduce consumer confusion and improve recycling rates.

The Recycled Materials Attribution and PACK Acts offer something the current recycling system has never had: one clear, national standard that consumers can trust, that businesses can build on and that communities can rely on. The solution is already on the table. Congress just needs to make it happen.

John Hewitt is senior vice president of the Consumer Brands Association and spokesperson for the Recycling Leadership Council.

articles.title: Harris endorses Pappas for New Hampshire Senate
articles.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris endorsed Rep. Chris Pappas (D) in the New Hampshire Senate race on Monday, marking the latest race in which the 2024 Democratic presidential candidate is lending her support ahead of November. “@KamalaHarris has stood tall for democracy and is committed to making this country fairer and freer for all. She…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris endorsed Rep. Chris Pappas (D) in the New Hampshire Senate race on Monday, marking the latest race in which the 2024 Democratic presidential candidate is lending her support ahead of November.

“@KamalaHarris has stood tall for democracy and is committed to making this country fairer and freer for all. She knows the stakes couldn’t be higher here in New Hampshire, and I’m proud to have her on Team Pappas,” Pappas wrote in a post on the social platform X.

The former vice president has weighed in on a handful of Senate and House races this midterm cycle, including supporting Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) in Georgia and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

While some members of the party have welcomed her support, others including Senate candidates Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) and Josh Turek (D-Iowa) as well as Iowa gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand have opted to keep Harris at arm’s length — which members of the party see as more of a commentary about the politics of red-leaning states than it is of Harris specifically.

Harris, meanwhile, narrowly won the Granite State in 2024 by close to 3 percentage points.

She’s also backed Democratic Senate candidates Roy Cooper in North Carolina, James Talarico in Texas and Troy Jackson in Maine, though the three have said little publicly about it.

Harris, who’s considering a 2028 White House bid, is not the only possible presidential hopeful weighing in on midterm races. Other top Democrats such as California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear are also wading into elections ahead of November.

articles.title: FCC Commissioner Calls Trump’s Comments On Kristen Welker A ‘Dangerous’ Threat To The Press
articles.summary: Trump said Welker should be 'rebuked or punished' for comments Sunday about the president's "mixed" record with political endorsements.
articles.body:
FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez says President Trump's repeated suggestions that journalists should be punished for saying things the president doesn't like "undermine the foundation of our democracy" and "these threats to press freedom are dangerous."

Trump has long attacked reporters as "enemies of the state," and he was angered Sunday by NBC's Kristen Welker, who said on Meet the Press that the president has had "some mixed results" with his endorsements of Republican candidates headed toward the decisive midterm elections.

'She will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment'

Calling Welker "the Unpopular 'Hostess' of the once great Meet the Press," Trump insisted his endorsed candidates had won 100% of contests for the U.S. Senate and 98% for the House. "How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves," he asked in a post on his Truth Social platform. "Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment."

Gomez, the only Democratic commissioner on the Federal Communications Commission, used her own post to remind the president that "the FCC has no authority to punish journalists this administration doesn't like."

Gomez has pushed back against the administration before, including speaking out about the FCC itself when Trump called on the FCC to target ABC for comments made by late night host Jimmy Kimmel.

"The FCC is once again targeting an administration critic by mob rule. Let's not pretend this FCC hasn't already made up its mind. All they want is for their pro-censorship partisan allies to nod in agreement. My message to Disney: Don't flinch. Fight," Gomez said in a post on X in May.

Gomez recently told The Hollywood Reporter that she hopes to be reconfirmed for another term as FCC commissioner--hers technically ended in June--as she believes it's essential that the commission remain a bipartisan body rather than a tool for the president to weaponize against his enemies.

" ​​I think it's important that we maintain somebody that pushes back against this administration's overreaches," she said.

As for Welker's comment that Trump has had a "mixed" record of endorsing candidates, it all depends on how you crunch the numbers. According to Ballotpedia , the president has endorsed 332 candidates in 2026, with a 96% success rate in primaries to date. Many were low-stakes races, and Trump missed with endorsements in far more consequential races, like his endorsement of Burt Jones for governor of Georgia and Randy Feenstra for governor of Iowa--both of whom lost their primary races.

Going back to last year, Trump's success rate with endorsements dropped to just 43%, with notable misses including the New Jersey governor's race and Trump's endorsement of Andrew Cuomo, who lost the New York City mayor's race to Zohran Mamdani.

The Commission met to discuss oversight of the FCC Lifeline program, broadband deployment on the 900 MHz band, capping noncommercial educational reserved FM band applications, and reforming intercarrier compensation. articles.title: Democratic FCC commissioner on Trump’s Kristen Welker threat: ‘Dangerous’
articles.summary: Anna Gomez, a Democratic commissioner for the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), on Sunday described President Trump’s threat to report NBC News’s Kristen Welker as “dangerous.” Trump signaled the “Meet the Press” host could face an FCC probe after she reportedly said candidates he endorsed have received mixed results during the midterm primary cycle. “As I’ve…
articles.body:
Anna Gomez, a Democratic commissioner for the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), on Sunday described President Trump’s threat to report NBC News’s Kristen Welker as “dangerous.”

Trump signaled the “Meet the Press” host could face an FCC probe after she reportedly said candidates he endorsed have received mixed results during the midterm primary cycle.

“As I’ve said many times, the FCC has no authority to punish journalists this administration doesn’t like,” Gomez wrote on the social platform X . “These threats to press freedom are dangerous. They undermine the foundation of our democracy, and they have no place in it.”

CNN’s Brian Stelter reported on social media that Welker talked about Trump’s “mixed” endorsement results during a preshow live shot on WRC-TV, NBC’s Washington, D.C., affiliate.

“He, of course, has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries,” the NBC host said. “He’s had some mixed results, but most recently, his pick of Sen. Darline Graham, of course, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was successful in her primary battle, so now she takes on Dr. Annie Andrews in South Carolina.”

Trump asked on Truth Social , in response to the remarks, “How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves?”

“Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment,” the president continued. “Unfortunately, she is not the only one. The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.'”

But some Republican candidates endorsed by Trump have lost their primary races, including Rep. Cory Mills (Fla.) in his reelection bid against Republican TV anchor Ryan Elijah. Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) and Michigan House candidate Amir Hassan (R) also lost their respective contests .

Trump has sparred with Welker before. The president abruptly ended an in-person interview with her in June after he claimed without evidence that the California gubernatorial primary was “rigged.”

His threat to report Welker to the FCC comes after Disney and ABC last week sued the agency , arguing that the Trump administration is attempting to censor journalists by urging the commission to conduct an early review of the news outlet’s broadcasting licenses.

“I have long called on companies to push back against this kind of government intimidation, and I’m glad Disney has shown courage and stepped up,” Gomez told MeidasTouch last week, praising that ABC “stepped up” to sue the FCC and FCC Commissioner Brendan Carr.

articles.title: Kalshi bans George Santos for life after he secretly bet on himself
articles.summary: The prediction marketplace platform Kalshi has hit former U.S. Congressman George Santos with its first-ever permanent ban.
articles.body: The prediction marketplace platform Kalshi has hit former U.S. Rep. George Santos with its first-ever lifetime ban after finding he bet against his own announced plans to attend President Donald Trump’s State of the Union address. “The Compliance Department found that Santos made these statements with the intent to manipulate the price of the Yes or No contracts that he intended to purchase. Ultimately, these statements did in fact manipulate the price of said contracts,” the company said. In addition to barring him from “direct or indirect access” to its platform, Kalshi fined Santos $71,356 — multiples of the $17,839.57 it said he made from his wagers. Kalshi said it hit him with extra penalties because of “his lack of cooperation” with its probe. Santos mocked the company in a post on X Monday, saying “thanks for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform. Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for.” An attorney for Santos did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Late last month, Santos, a former Republican congressman from New York, agreed to pay $35,000 to settle a federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission investigation into his suspicious trades. The CFTC found that Santos had “made a series of material misrepresentations and omissions” in his social media posts about whether he would attend the State of the Union while placing bets on his own attendance. Santos’ attorney, Joseph Murray, said he’d agree to pay to “put this matter behind” him and had not admitted any wrongdoing. “He chose a prompt, practical resolution, rather than protracted, costly litigation, and that choice should not be mistaken for admission of any wrongdoing, because it is not one,” Murray said then in a statement Santos shared on X. Santos had taken to X back in February to tell his millions of followers that he planned to attend Trump’s speech. “I’m gonna be in the gallery,” Santos said in a video on X. Santos did not attend the event. “I guess people lost money,” Santos said on his podcast in March. “Some people made unexpected money. That’s to show you how fragile these markets are.” Santos, who was revealed to have fabricated large swaths of his background during his congressional campaign, was expelled from Congress while under federal investigation for fraud in 2023. He pleaded guilty in 2024 to federal charges including wire fraud, identity theft and money laundering. He was sentenced to seven years in prison and ordered to pay almost $374,000 in restitution and over $200,000 in forfeiture. Trump commuted Santos’ sentence after he’d been behind bars for three months, saying he had been “horribly mistreated.” “Good luck George, have a great life!” the president wrote on Truth Social.

articles.title: El-Sayed tries to make peace with Jewish Democrats but draws line at dumping Hasan Piker
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed met with Michigan's Democratic Jewish Caucus to apologize, but Mike Rogers calls his remarks a "sham apology" amid antisemitism concerns.
articles.body: Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed spent this past weekend trying to mend fences with Jewish Democrats in Michigan, but his Republican rival calls El-Sayed's comments a "sham apology." El-Sayed, in an appearance Saturday before the Michigan Democrats' Jewish Caucus, and in an answer to a question from Fox News Digital, apologized for comments he made after a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue. But he pushed back when asked to repudiate controversial comments from incendiary left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who is a strong supporter of his campaign. A vocal critic of Israel who describes its military actions against Hamas in Gaza as "genocide," El-Sayed is facing off against former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee in the Great Lakes battleground state, for a crucial open Senate seat the Democrats must hold in the midterm elections as they aim to win back control of the chamber. El-Sayed's narrow primary victory over more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in what was a divisive intraparty showdown was arguably the biggest victory to date for the left in its battle against the establishment for the ideological future of the Democratic Party. El-Sayed appeared this past weekend at the state party's nominating convention in Lansing, Michigan in an effort to unify Democrats in the wake of the primary battle. DEMOCRATIC MICHIGAN AG ACCUSES HER PARTY OF 'ABSOLUTELY NOT' DOING ENOUGH TO COUNTER ANTISEMITISM Fox News Digital asked El-Sayed about a recent controversy stemming from comments he made in response to an attack on a Michigan synagogue, when federal investigators say a gunman inspired and radicalized by Hezbollah crashed into the place of worship seeking to kill as many Jewish people as he could. The alleged attacker was a Lebanese-born man who a week earlier had lost relatives in an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon. "Hurt people, hurt people," El-Sayed said in response to the attack. He was criticized by members of his own party, including Michigan Secretary of State Dana Nessel, who discussed the comments in a recent interview with The Atlantic, and declined to attend this past weekend's convention partly over concerns of antisemitism in the Democratic Party. El-Sayed told Fox News Digital his comments "might have been misconstrued to be justifying something I did not intend to justify," but then offered an apology. "To anybody who feels like my comments may have been hurtful, I’m really sorry. That was not my intention. We condemned that terrorist attack. We condemned it outright," El-Sayed added. "What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn’t the time for context and you don’t ever want to trample somebody’s pain." El-Sayed is an epidemiologist and former Wayne County Health Department director who, if elected in November, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. He has argued against unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel, as have other progressive politicians. And El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to directly answer whether Israel has the right to exist. He said his message to Jewish voters in Michigan is, "We may not agree on everything when it comes to foreign policy... I'm not going to stop fighting for Palestinian self-determination... but that does not mean that I will not stand up… for safety for all communities and I believe in the safety and dignity of Jewish kids like I believe in the safety and dignity of my own kids." Before taking questions from reporters, El-Sayed met in Lansing with the state's Democratic Jewish Caucus. "He just had a very good meeting with us," Daniel Rivkin, a convention delegate and member of the caucus, told Fox News Digital, as he referred to El-Sayed. "We're having real conversations." CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLL IN MICHIGAN'S BLOCKBUSTER SENATE RACE The El-Sayee campaign is also in the process of hiring a Jewish liaison, Fox News Digital confirmed on Monday. But some Jewish leaders in Michigan went public on Saturday with an open letter urging Jewish Democrats and independents in the state to sign their names in support of Rogers, who is making a second straight run for the Senate after falling just 20,000 votes short in 2024. "Many of us have been fiercely supportive of Democratic candidates and principles. All of us have felt threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed, which has included demonization of Jews, equivocation on terrorism, exclusion of Jewish Americans from public life, and expression of implacable hatred of the world’s only Jewish nation," the letter stated. Rogers, in a statement highlighting the letter, claimed that "Abdul El-Sayed fans the flames of antisemitism. We’re fighting to extinguish it." In an interview Monday morning on Fox News' "Fox and Friends," Rogers said, "We've had so many Democrat Jewish people here in the state of Michigan ring up our phone and say, "I can't do this. I'm for you." WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW Referring to El-Sayed, Rogers said, "When someone says you might have been offended by what I said, that's not an apology." And he claimed that El-Sayed "has a long history of antisemitic and inflammatory comments." But El-Sayed has repeatedly pushed back, saying, "My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own kids. We have a responsibility to take on antisemitism in all of its forms, wherever we see it." Making El-Sayed's mission to make peace with Jewish Democrats and independents more difficult is the backing he receives from Piker. Piker recently featured on his stream an image of state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee in Michigan's 11th Congressional District. Moss, who is Jewish, has said that people are sharing a fake audio clip of him claiming that his entire reason for running for Congress is to make sure that America continues to support Israel. "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker warned. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Piker, who endorsed El-Sayed for the Democratic nomination and appeared at some of the candidate's campaign events including a primary night party in Detroit, has repeatedly stood by his numerous past comments critical of Israel over its ongoing war against Hamas in Gaza. El-Sayed, who over the past week appeared to try and distance himself from Piker, responded to the firestorm by saying, "I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople." On Saturday, El-Sayed was peppered with questions from reporters about Piker. "We’re in the state of Michigan. If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you’re missing the boat," El-Sayed told reporters. "This is about affordability in Michigan. This is about seeing a doctor in Michigan. This is about Donald Trump’s disastrous policies in Michigan. That’s what I’m focused on right now." As the questions about Piker continued, El-Sayed repeatedly characterized him as "a streamer from California" who is irrelevant to his race in Michigan. "This is not a serious conversation." THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE Besides his numerous antisemitic comments, Piker is known for saying "America deserved 9/11," praising Mao Zedong and Communist China, and arguing that capitalists should be murdered in the streets. The Democrats' discord over Israel comes as most GOP leaders continue to showcase their support for Israeli leaders. As the Republican Jewish Coalition's annual leadership summit got underway Sunday evening in Las Vegas, El-Sayed and the far-left drew boos from the audience of high-powered GOP activists and donors. Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters, speaking Monday at the RJC gathering, said that "the same hatred that fueled" the Oct. 7, 2023 large-scale attack by Hamas on Israel that killed about 1,200 people and triggered the ongoing war "is growing right here in our backyard." "It has found a home in the Democratic Party. This did not happen overnight. It happened step-by-step as radical extremists took over the party, and the Democratic leaders let them," Gruters argued. Meanwhile, there's no letup in the battle between the left and the center for the future of the Democratic Party. Rahm Emanuel, a former ambassador, congressman, Chicago mayor and former White House chief of staff to then-President Barack Obama, took aim at the socialist push taking aim at the party's establishment. "The Democratic Party is not open to being taken over," Emanuel, who's seriously mulling a 2028 White House run, told Fox News' Shannon Bream on "Fox News Sunday." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I don't consider the Democratic Socialists are part of the Democratic Party. About four weeks ago, they had a convention in Chicago. Separate party. They believe in defunding police, letting prisoners out of prison, opening borders, eliminating the Pentagon. If you're so confident people want that, I'll see you in November. Put it on the ballot. Let's go. Run as a separate party," Emanuel emphasized. Democratic Party leaders, when asked about the party's current ideological warfare, often point to Democrats as a "big tent" party. But veteran Democratic strategist Julian Epstein criticizes such responses and jabs at his party for failing to call out the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). "They’ve taken cover behind the empty 'Big Tent" lie as radical DSA members and allies, like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Colorado’s Melat Kiros, triumph in Democratic primaries," Epstein wrote in an opinion piece last week in the New York Post. Epstein, who served as chief counsel for the Democratic minority on the House Judiciary Committee during the 1998 impeachment proceeds against then-President Bill Clinton and who later served on Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign, argued, "Moderates should unite and shed the Big Tent delusion — because they have nothing to lose but their chains." Jeff Crank, R-Colo., introduced a measure Thursday condemning socialism in all its forms, telling Fox News Digital he wanted to use the vote to force moderate House Democrats to take a more public stance against the DSA. articles.title: Ex-congressman George Santos banned from betting platform Kalshi  for life
articles.summary: The prediction market operator Kalshi says Santos made barred trades and misleading comments that influenced prices.
articles.body:
Prediction-market operator Kalshi has permanently barred former US congressman George Santos from trading on its platform.

The company alleged that Santos, who was expelled from Congress following a series of fraud and identity-theft charges, placed bets in February related to his own attendance at US President Donald Trump's State of the Union address, according to a notice of disciplinary action.

Kalshi said its compliance team concluded his activity showed signs of insider dealing, prompting the lifetime ban. It said it was acting independently without waiting for external enforcement action.

Santos on X thanked Kalshi for the ban and said "Let's see how much longer you guys are around for".

The BBC has contacted Santos for comment.

In 2025, Trump ordered the release of Santos, who had been sentenced to a seven-year prison term for wire fraud and identity theft. He had served three months.

In July, Santos agreed to pay $35,000 to settle a federal investigation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission into his State of the Union trades.

Kalshi, alleging Santos used non-public information to place bets, issued a penalty of $71,356 (£38,000).

The disciplinary moves come at a moment when prediction markets – which allow users to wager on outcomes ranging from elections to economic indicators – are facing heightened scrutiny.

Both Kalshi and rival Polymarket have reported an uptick in unusual trading patterns, forcing platforms to strengthen monitoring systems and respond more aggressively to potential misconduct.

Kalshi said Santos's case was referred to federal authorities earlier this summer after internal systems flagged suspicious behaviour linked to his account.

The company said the case centered on his trades in a market tied to whether he would attend Trump's address – an event he could directly influence.

Its compliance team found he placed a series of sizeable bets between 2 and 25 February, some of which were based on false or misleading public statements about his plans, according to the company.

His comments moved contract prices, and he ultimately earned $17,839.57 from the trades.

Santos has denied wrongdoing in various matters but has admitted to stealing identities of nearly a dozen people, including next of kin. He pleaded guilty to wire fraud and aggravated identity theft and served three months in prison before Trump commuted his sentence last year.

He embellished much about his biography in the run-up to his election to Congress in 2022. The former lawmaker was only the sixth in US history to be expelled from Congress.

The Kalshi episode underscores the growing compliance burden facing prediction markets as they attract more users and move closer to mainstream products. Regulators have signalled that platforms will be expected to meet higher standards as the industry matures, particularly when political or economic events are involved.

articles.title: ‘Backwards and poor’: Trump issues dire warning to communities blocking critical technology
articles.summary: President Donald Trump warned communities rejecting data centers risk becoming "backwards and poor" as states battle over AI boom energy and water costs.
articles.body: President Donald Trump took aim Monday at the growing backlash against data centers, warning that communities that shut the door on the facilities risk missing out on the jobs and economic gains of America's AI boom. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," he added. Trump has made energy dominance and U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence central pillars of his second term, placing data centers at the center of his push to maintain America's edge over China. "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement," Trump wrote, arguing that resistance to new facilities risks undercutting America's edge in the global AI race. ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI The data center boom has also emerged as a midterm flashpoint, as concerns over rising electricity costs, water use and rapid development collide with promises of jobs, investment and U.S. dominance in artificial intelligence. That tension is already playing out across the country. Trump has specifically criticized Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's approach, calling the Lone Star State's stance toward data centers a "mistake" and pointing to the economic investment the projects can bring to communities willing to host them. Texas has cemented its status as a heavyweight in the industry, with Dallas ranking as the world's No. 1 primary data center market in Cushman & Wakefield's 2026 Global Data Center Market Comparison. But billions of dollars in new investment have also brought enormous electricity demands and questions over who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support the boom. Abbott has moved to address those concerns, directing regulators to ensure data centers cover the infrastructure costs needed to serve them and calling on developers to add their own power generation rather than shift costs onto Texas residents. A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD'S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES Meanwhile, in Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro recently imposed new requirements on large data center developments. Other governors have taken a more restrictive stance. Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyper-scale data centers as states grapple with concerns over electricity costs, grid reliability and the pace of development. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Data centers house the servers and computing equipment that power artificial intelligence and cloud services, requiring vast amounts of electricity to operate and cool. Most Americans may never see the inside of one, but they rely on data centers constantly, often without realizing it. The growing patchwork of state restrictions and requirements could complicate Trump’s push for rapid data center expansion as communities weigh America’s AI ambitions against concerns over electricity costs, water use and development.

articles.title: El-Sayed torched online after brushing off questions about Hasan Piker campaign ties: ‘What a pal’
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed dismissed Hasan Piker as just "a single streamer from California," despite inviting him to stump on the Michigan campaign trail.
articles.body: Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is facing a wave of online blowback after dodging questions about his ties to far-left streamer Hasan Piker, a frequent presence on the campaign trail in Michigan. When asked about Piker’s influence on his campaign, El-Sayed told reporters the race is about Michigan and that he is "not interested in a conversation about a social media person in California." "But I don’t want to have a conversation about a Twitch streamer in California," El-Sayed said. "This is not a serious conversation." Fox News Digital then pressed El-Sayed on why he brought Piker to Michigan if that was the case, which he waved off before doubling down and calling Piker "a single streamer from California" when another reporter asked if he would condemn him. ABDUL EL-SAYED PLAYS DOWN HASAN PIKER TIES AFTER STREAMER’S VIRAL ANTISEMITISM FIRESTORM The clip exploded across social media and drew widespread ridicule as El-Sayed scrambles to distance himself from the streamer, who has roughly 10 million social media followers. In a post on X, writer and political commentator Stephen L. Miller wrote, "Amazing. They are so terrified of him that she literally jumps in one question deep." "Who is the candidate here?" Miller wrote in another post. "This keeps getting worse," Republican political strategist Kyle Martinsen posted on X. "I’m interested in it so there’s a problem here," Townhall senior columnist Kurt Schlichter posted on X. In another post on X, "The Charlie Kirk Show" executive producer Andrew Kolvet wrote, "It's very clear Abul El Sayed is panicking. He went from doing a half dozen campaign stops with Hasan Piker and taking glamor shots with him, to refusing to say his name. Now he's just ‘some media person in California.’ What a pal." HASAN PIKER INSISTS ABDUL EL-SAYED ASKED HIM TO 'STUMP' FOR MICHIGAN CAMPAIGN AMID BACKLASH "He might be worse than Kamala…," Fox News contributor Joe Concha posted on X. Pro-Israel activist and philanthropist Adam Milstein also wrote in a post on X, "El Sayed again refuses to condemn Hasan Piker — who himself recently confirmed it was El Sayed that asked him to campaign for him, not the reverse." Piker has emerged as a growing flashpoint within the Democratic Party over his past controversial remarks, including his claim that "America deserved 9/11." Last week, El-Sayed responded to outrage over his association with Piker after the streamer's comments on a viral audio clip involving Jewish Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee in the state’s 11th Congressional District, sparked outrage. "I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople," El-Sayed said in a statement. EL-SAYED PALS AROUND WITH FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER THE DAY BEFORE CRUCIAL MICHIGAN SENATE ELECTION Despite El-Sayed’s attempts to distance himself from Piker, the streamer has spoken openly about his invitation to join the campaign, saying at an April rally with El-Sayed, "The reason why, when Abdul asked for me to come on this journey with him, I said yes, absolutely." In a Friday interview with Semafor columnist David Weigel, Piker said El-Sayed also asked him to "stump" for his campaign. El-Sayed will face Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers for retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters’ seat in a race that could determine control of the Senate. articles.title: Trump admin revives ‘Apprentice’-era energy with $1M business battle in DC
articles.summary: Nicki Minaj, Grant Cardone, and Joe Gebbia will judge the SBA's Patriot Pitch as five entrepreneur finalists compete for $1 million in cash.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The Small Business Administration is bringing a celebrity panel to Washington next month to judge five entrepreneurs competing for a share of a $1 million prize pool, Fox News Digital has exclusively learned. "As our nation marks its 250th anniversary, the SBA is celebrating America’s legacy of free enterprise through the Million Dollar Pitch Competition—a historic live event showcasing the essential contributions of America’s small businesses," SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler told Fox News Digital. Rapper Nicki Minaj, entrepreneur and private equity fund manager Grant Cardone, co-founder of Airbnb and U.S. Chief Design Office Joe Gebbia will judge the final competition. REP ROGER WILLIAMS: 250 YEARS OF HARD WORK PAYS OFF FOR MAIN STREET BUSINESSES The competition is another example of the Trump administration’s efforts to spotlight American ingenuity and partner with the private sector to support innovation and small-business growth, Fox News Digital learned. I look forward to joining them next month as we recognize the innovators and job creators who power American strength," Loeffler added. The participants were evaluated based on categories of strengthening American competitiveness, examples of small businesses "punching above its weight," economic impact and quality jobs and business fundamentals and execution readiness. articles.title: DSA leader's working-class image takes hit as public records pile up contradictions
articles.summary: Gustavo Gordillo, NYC Democratic Socialists of America co-chair, faces scrutiny over claims about his immigrant parents, union status and housing.
articles.body: The contradictions are piling up around New York City Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Gustavo Gordillo, whose claims about his working-class credentials — from being a "union electrician" to his housing and family story — have increasingly collided with public records and other evidence. Gordillo has repeatedly invoked his family’s immigrant success story while explaining his support for socialism. "My parents came here, they had nothing," Gordillo told the New York Times in a profile piece earlier this month. "Their first jobs were in fast food and cleaning houses. They built success in this country. And they’re absolutely the exception." According to Gordillo, he advances the cause of socialism because he believes it can "build a world" where his parents’ success story is "not exceptional." LUXURY TRAVEL, SHOPPING, SIX-FIGURE INCOME: BATTLEGROUND DEMS RIPPED FOR 'PHONY' WORKING-CLASS NARRATIVE A 2021 obituary for Gordillo’s paternal grandfather, however, raises questions about the family history behind that account. Manuel Gordillo, Gordillo’s grandfather, immigrated from Peru to the United States to practice medicine in 1958. After settling in the United States, Manuel met his future wife in St. Louis, and the couple later had Gordillo’s father, Gustavo. The obituary also notes that Gordillo’s grandfather built a successful life as a psychiatrist in Ohio, at one point serving as the president of the Ohio Psychiatric Association, casting doubt on the socialist’s claim that his parents grew up in poverty. "My dad, his first job in the United States was working at Wendy’s, my mom’s first job was a house cleaner, and they did make a living for themselves, and they had success," Gordillo told Fox News in July. Gordillo and the New York City Democratic Socialists of America did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday. The questions surrounding Gordillo’s account of his family history come after discrepancies emerged over how he has described his occupation and living arrangements. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST HEADED FOR $142K LEGISLATURE SALARY BEGS FOR RENT HANDOUT, DELETES POST AFTER BACKLASH The 38-year-old socialist, for example, told the New York Times that he was renting a modest apartment in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn only for it to be revealed that he was actually living in a $1.4 million townhouse owned by his father in a trendier part of the borough. "Not only did DSA co-chair Gustavo Gordillo's parents buy him this rowhouse, they converted it from a two family and renovated it into a luxury single-family home for him," New York City Councilwoman Vickie Paladino said on X. "Exactly the kind of 'greed' the DSA rails against on a daily basis, and reducing valuable housing inventory by one more unit, which is supposedly something the DSA cares very deeply about." FRUSTRATED BLUE-COLLAR UNION BOSSES RIP SOCIALIST POLITICIANS, WARN OF LABOR EXODUS FROM DEM PARTY Also undercutting Gordillo’s working-class image is his continued self-identification as a "union electrician" despite the fact that he hasn’t been a member of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers since March, when he was fired for not showing up to his apprenticeship. "After learning of Mr. Gordillo’s prolonged absence from and failure to participate in required work and classes, the trustees of the Joint Apprentice Training Committee terminated Mr. Gordillo from the program," the IBEW said in a statement. articles.title: Vance characterizes Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed as ‘evil’
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance described Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic nominee for Senate, as “evil” during a campaign rally.
articles.body: STERLING HEIGHTS, Mich. — Vice President JD Vance described Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic nominee for Senate, as “evil” during a campaign rally here Monday. “I realize that there’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today,” said Vance, addressing several hundred people at an event put on by MAGA Inc., a super PAC closely aligned with President Donald Trump. “And it’s people who see themselves not as citizens of a common nation fighting for every single person — whether they’re Jewish or Christian, whether they’re white or Black or brown — but see themselves as fighting for one group at the expense of others, and that is how, ladies and gentlemen, you destroy the United States of America,” Vance added. El-Sayed, who is Muslim, recently apologized for his response after an attack on a Michigan synagogue in March. In a video he posted to social media then, El-Sayed condemned the attack while adding that “hurt people hurt people” — comments that critics have characterized as wrongly empathetic toward someone who violently targeted Jewish people. “My comments may have been misconstrued to justify something I did not mean to justify,” El-Sayed said last week. Vance referred to that episode Monday, as well as El-Sayed’s alliance with Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer who previously said on a livestream that “America deserved 9/11.” Piker has since apologized for the remark, which El-Sayed called “dumb” this month during an appearance on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” after winning the Democratic primary. El-Sayed faces former Rep. Mike Rogers, who also spoke at Monday’s rally, in a November election that could determine partisan control of the Senate. The seat is open because Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking a third term. “When I see Abdul El-Sayed campaign around the state with somebody who said that America deserved 9/11, what I see is a man who has sympathy and compassion for people who share his religion but have nothing for people who don’t, a person who will apologize for a murderer so long as he looks the right way, but will not understand the plight of an innocent child if that person has their own faith,” Vance said. “And that is the root of this terrible evil, I believe, in the United States of America that is on the rise.” He added: “Today, you have an opportunity to speak loudly, and in November you have an opportunity to speak much more loudly against the hatred that is on the rise in the United States of America. Reject Abdul El-Sayed.” El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to Vance’s attacks. The MAGA Inc. event, staged inside a warehouse for a local electric services contractor and tree-trimming company, featured banners that read “Protecting Americans.” It was the super PAC’s first major midterm rally to feature Vance, a likely presidential contender in 2028, as a headliner. At least one attendee Monday sported a red “VANCE 2028” baseball cap. MAGA Inc. recently spent to boost Trump-endorsed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., in a Senate primary runoff, but there has been skepticism in the broader GOP campaign universe over how engaged the organization will be in key races this fall. One Republican strategist who is involved in Senate races and was granted anonymity to speak candidly said they doubted MAGA Inc. would spend heavily on the midterms. They noted that the group has not yet spent much of its money. “It should be called the MAGA Library Fund,” this person said. “That’s where that money is going to go by and large.” Vance’s visit also came amid a tense trade war between the U.S. and Canada. The clash is acutely felt in Michigan, which exports 39% of its goods to Canada, according to data compiled by the Progressive Policy Institute, a left-leaning think tank. The vice president did not mention the matter, focusing instead on the administration’s anti-fraud efforts, which he leads, and Michigan’s competitive political races. He also announced a new White House crackdown on fraudulent truck drivers — an effort Vance said is aimed at rooting out undocumented immigrants and workers who don’t speak English. Vance also advocated for Rep. John James, the Republican candidate for governor, and military veteran Mike Bouchard, the GOP nominee to succeed James in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District. James is competing with Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee, in the race to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Bouchard is running against Democrat Christina Hines, a former special victims prosecutor. But Vance reserved his most heated rhetoric for the Senate race, where he encouraged Michigan voters to give Rogers a chance even if they don’t agree with him “100% of the time.” In a parting shot, Vance referred to a recent social media post from El-Sayed about second lady Usha Vance. El-Sayed, playing off Vance’s remarks about his grandfather at an event in Ohio this month, mockingly wondered if the vice president would take his wife back in time to meet him. “I actually think that the people of Michigan think it’s kind of weird when you talk about another guy’s wife,” Vance said. “But whatever you want to talk about, Abdul, keep my wife’s name the hell out of your mouth.”

articles.title: Supreme Court allows Trump to move forward with White House ballroom construction
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday handed a win to President Donald Trump by allowing him to move forward indefinitely with the construction of his new White House ballroom.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday handed a win to President Donald Trump by allowing him to move forward indefinitely with the construction of his new White House ballroom. The court, divided 5-4, granted an emergency request filed by the Trump administration, blocking lower court rulings that would have put the aboveground portion of the project on hold. This followed an interim decision along similar lines issued by Chief Justice John Roberts on Aug. 21. The legal challenge was brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which argued that the president did not have unilateral authority to proceed with construction. In the unsigned ruling, the court said that the trust likely does not have legal standing to bring the underlying lawsuit. The court did not reach any conclusion on whether Trump has authority to carry out construction without congressional approval. Roberts joined the court’s three liberal justices in dissent. “Construction of the ballroom has proceeded apace for the better part of a year. That construction is likely unlawful,” Roberts wrote. The administration has said in court filings that construction was 65% complete as of Aug. 24, with a 250-person crew working 20 hours a day, seven days a week. The White House has said the $400 million project will be funded entirely by private donations, an assertion that has been widely disputed. Secret Service funds have already been directed to cover some of the project’s security enhancements. The overall plan includes an extensive underground component, including secure locations and medical facilities that the administration has argued are needed for security. A federal judge had ruled in favor of the trust, saying that while the underground construction could move forward, the ballroom itself could not be built while litigation continued. On Aug. 7, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld that decision. The trust’s claim for standing hinges on a declaration made by member Alison Hoagland, a preservationist who lives in Washington and serves on the organization’s board of trustees. Hoagland regularly walks by the White House, adding that she would “suffer both professional and personal injuries, including to my aesthetic, cultural and historical interests, if a ballroom of the proposed form and scale were constructed.” The trust argued that the government had no authority to build the ballroom under a federal law that requires the “express authority of Congress” to build on federal land in Washington, D.C. But the Trump administration countered that other provisions of federal law allow the president to undertake improvements on the White House grounds.
